text: The internet ran out of addresses.
Not in theory.
On the third of February, twenty eleven, the last free blocks were handed out, at a ceremony in Miami.
And yet you're watching this.
Your phone is online. So is your TV, your laptop, maybe even your fridge.
So how does an internet with no addresses left keep growing?
The answer involves a guess from nineteen seventy-seven, a trick hiding in your router,
a market where addresses sell for twenty dollars each, and a fix that took thirty years.
Every device on the internet needs an address, like a phone number, so data knows where to go.
In nineteen seventy-seven, Vint Cerf, one of the engineers who designed the internet's core protocols,
had to decide how long those addresses would be.
Some colleagues wanted a hundred and twenty-eight bits. Others called that crazy. Cerf picked thirty-two.
Here's the reasoning. They needed a few bits to say which network you're on.
How many countries were there? Nobody knew, and there was no Google to check.
So they guessed a hundred and twenty-eight, doubled it for room, and got two hundred and fifty-six networks. That's eight bits.
The other twenty-four bits named the computer inside each network.
Thirty-two bits gives you two to the thirty-second power: about four point three billion addresses,
roughly one for every person on Earth at the time. For a research experiment, that was enormous.
Cerf has joked about it ever since. His summary: it was enough for an experiment.
The problem is, the experiment never ended.
For years, addresses were handed out generously.
Early companies and universities got blocks of nearly seventeen million addresses each.
Then came the web, then broadband, then smartphones.
The world's address pool is managed by an organisation called I-A-N-A,
which hands big blocks to five regional registries:
North America, Europe, Asia-Pacific, Latin America and Africa.
Each block is one two-hundred-and-fifty-sixth of all I P version four addresses.
At the end of January twenty eleven, I-A-N-A gave two of its last blocks to Asia-Pacific. That left five.
A policy agreed years earlier kicked in: one final block for each region.
On the third of February, they were handed out. The central pool was empty.
Then the regions ran dry, one by one. Asia-Pacific within ten weeks.
Europe rationed its last block for years, handing out tiny slices,
until the twenty-fifth of November, twenty nineteen, when it made its final allocation and announced it had completely run out.
So how are billions of new devices still getting online? Look at your router.
Your home probably has one public address, the one the rest of the internet sees.
Every device inside gets a private address instead, from ranges that are reused in millions of homes at once.
That's why so many home networks use addresses starting with one nine two, dot, one six eight.
When your phone asks a website for something, the router swaps your phone's private address for the home's public one,
and writes down a port number to remember who asked.
When the answer comes back, it checks its table and passes the answer to your phone.
This is network address translation, or nat. One public address, dozens of devices.
It works so well that many internet providers now do it a second time, sharing one public address across many customers.
That's called carrier-grade nat.
But it has a cost. Devices behind nat can't easily be reached from the outside.
It's why some online games complain about a strict nat type, why hosting a server at home can be a headache, and why peer-to-peer apps need clever workarounds.
Scarcity did something else: it gave addresses a price.
Companies with spare blocks sell them to companies that need them, through the registries' official transfer process.
In twenty twenty-six, the average price has been around twenty dollars per address.
A small block of two hundred and fifty-six addresses costs several thousand dollars.
Prices have actually fallen over the past year. But the market exists because the old system is full.
The real fix was designed in the nineteen-nineties: I P version six. Instead of thirty-two bits, it uses a hundred and twenty-eight.
That isn't four times as many addresses. Each extra bit doubles the count,
so it's two to the hundred-and-twenty-eighth: about three hundred and forty undecillion.
That's thirty-four followed by thirty-seven zeros. Enough to give every grain of sand on Earth billions of billions of addresses each.
An I P version six address looks different too: groups of hexadecimal digits separated by colons.
So why didn't everyone just switch? Because I P version six can't talk directly to version four. They're separate languages.
Every website, router, phone and app had to learn the new one while keeping the old one running.
For years, nobody wanted to go first.
Websites didn't bother because users weren't on I P version six, and providers didn't bother because websites weren't.
And nat made the pain bearable, so the deadline kept slipping.
But it kept moving. Mobile networks adopted it early, because they had millions of new phones and no addresses to give them.
In several countries, most users already connect over I P version six.
And in March twenty twenty-six, something symbolic happened:
for the first time, Google measured more than half of its users reaching it over I P version six.
Fifty point one percent, on the twenty-eighth of March.
So, did the internet run out of addresses? Yes. In twenty eleven, and then in region after region.
But it didn't stop. It bent.
One address shared by a whole home, then by a whole neighbourhood, while a far bigger address system was slowly built alongside.
Your phone may well be using both right now.
One decision from nineteen seventy-seven still shapes how every device you own connects.
Vint Cerf's own summary is still the best one: it was enough for an experiment. The experiment just never ended.
